catalog_quote: Stress is phonemic in Batuley. Although stress most often falls on the penultimate syllable of a word, it is not entirely predictable. Furthermore, there are at least two minimal pair sets whose words are distinguished on the basis of stress, as shown in (49a-b) and (50a-b). (49) a. /ˈtaɸur/ [ˈta.ɸur] ‘papeda’ (i.e., ‘sago congee’) b. /taˈɸur/ [ta.ˈɸur] ‘shelled mollusc’ (50) a. /ˈkaliŋ/ [ˈka.liŋ] ‘skin/body-1SG.POSS’ b. / kaˈliŋ/ [ka.ˈliŋ] ‘fishing line’ Affixes are not usually stressed. Stress predominately only falls on the root. In (51a-c), stress falls on the verb root. [...] [§2.9.2.2, p. 59:] Stress is phonemic in Batuley (see §2.6 above). So far, there appear to be only two minimal pairs where a difference in stress placement alone distinguishes meaning. ... Further investigation into representing stress and the effects of stress is greatly required.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive (marked in phonemic transcriptions throughout), with a strong default on the penultimate syllable; stress stays on the root and affixes are normally unstressed; a minority of roots carry final stress (e.g. /taˈɸur/, /kaˈliŋ/, /naˈwaj/, /tuˈbaj/). Irregular verbs with fused prefix+root take initial stress except polysyllabic 2PL forms, which take final stress (2.7.1.2, pp. 34-35).
new_statements.secondary_stress: When primary stress shifts rightward in compounds, attributive constructions, reduplication or pronoun+verb phrases, the formerly primary-stressed syllable keeps secondary stress (e.g. /ˈaw ˈtaj/ -> [ˌaw ˈtaj]; /naˈwaj ˈlus/ -> [na.ˌwej.ˈlus]) and its /a/ dissimilates to [e] (2.2.2.4, pp. 16-17; 2.6.2, pp. 31-32). No statement of rhythmic secondary stress within simple words.
new_statements.exceptions: Two stress minimal pairs; final-stressed roots; 2PL forms of irregular fused verbs stress the final syllable (mi.ˈnam etc.); pronouns /ˈnaj/, /ˈkaem/ lose stress before a verb unless emphasised; author flags that stress 'has not been dealt with extensively' (2.10) and 'further investigation.. is greatly required' (2.9.2.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the phonological word (root plus affixes) in citation/elicited forms; 2.6.2 separately treats compound and phrasal (clause-level) primary stress, where the rightmost element takes primary stress. Variety described: Kabalsiang and Benjuring (northern Batuley villages).
new_statements.identity_note: Daigle 2015 describes the Batuley of the two northernmost villages, Kabalsiang and Benjuring (Aru Islands); he notes minor accent/vocabulary differences among the seven Batuley villages. Language-level glottocode batu1258 (no dialect subcodes in Glottolog); Mariri (mari1429), once treated by Hughes 1987 as a divergent Batuley dialect, is NOT covered.
